segments.say: Think of the smallest unit of social media: a like. A tiny thumb or a heart, a single tap. It carries almost no information, and yet many people check their counts, feel a lift when the number is high, and feel a small sting when it isn't. Psychologists have wondered whether a like works as a social reward in the brain.

Human beings are intensely social. For most of our history, being accepted by the group was a matter of survival, and a rejection could be dangerous. It would be surprising if our brains didn't treat signs of approval as rewards, and signs of disapproval as threats. The likes just make those signs countable.

At the University of California, Los Angeles, Lauren Sherman and her colleagues invited thirty-two teenagers into a brain scanner. They showed them a series of photos, one hundred and forty-eight in all, on a mock photo-sharing app. Each image appeared with a number of likes, supposedly from other teens, though the numbers were assigned by the researchers.

show.what: The power of the like in adolescence: effects of peer influence on neural and behavioral responses to social media

segments.say: The teenagers also saw some of their own photos, again with likes that the researchers had assigned. So the brain scans could compare what happened when a photo was popular, and when it wasn't, while the real quality of the photo was kept out of the picture. It's a neat way of isolating the effect of the number itself.

show.title: Teenagers in the UCLA scan
show.label: shown 148 photos, some with many likes and some with few

segments.say: When the teenagers saw their own photos with many likes, regions linked to reward were more active, including the nucleus accumbens, a region that is involved in many kinds of reward, from food to money to praise. Areas involved in social cognition and attention also responded. In plain language, a high number of likes lit up circuits that normally respond to things we value.

show.sub: Brain regions that respond to reward

segments.say: That last point is subtle and fascinating. The teenagers were more inclined to like photos that already had many likes, whatever the content. A like, in other words, doesn't only reward the person who gets it. It also shapes what the next viewer thinks about the photo.

show.title: What the UCLA scan suggested
items: Own photos with many likes drew a stronger response
Teenagers were also more likely to like popular photos themselves
The number of likes shaped judgement

segments.say: It's worth slowing down here. Thirty-two teenagers is a small sample. The scanner session is not the same as real life, and the likes were fake. The study also can't tell us whether any of this is harmful, or whether it differs from the thrill of a compliment in person. What it does show is that the social meaning of a number can be strong enough to be visible in the brain.

It also helps to remember that none of this is new. In earlier research, scientists found that being included, praised or valued activates similar reward regions, whether it happens online or in a room full of people. The likes are a new form, and the underlying machinery is ancient.

Naomi Eisenberger and colleagues asked people to play a simple ball-tossing game on a screen while in a scanner. Partway through, the other players stopped throwing to them. The participants showed activity in a region called the anterior cingulate cortex, which is also involved in the distress of physical pain. The study has been highly influential, though later work has argued that the overlap with physical pain is more complicated than first claimed.

show.what: Does rejection hurt? An fMRI study of social exclusion

segments.say: If being left out of a game can register in the brain as distress, then it isn't far-fetched to think that a post that no one reacts to can feel unpleasant. Many people describe exactly that: a post that gets little response, followed by the urge to delete it. The social pain system doesn't care that the exclusion is only a number.

Each of those four features adds something. The first is old, the second is new, the third echoes the pigeons, and the fourth adds a social loop. Together, they make a very strong signal from a very small tap.

show.title: Why likes matter to us
items: We are wired to care about acceptance
Counts make approval visible and comparable
They shape what other people think too

segments.say: A natural question follows. If likes are so powerful, what happens if you hide them? In 2019, Instagram tested hiding like counts in several countries, and some researchers, as well as the platforms, were curious about the effects on users. The results were less dramatic than many people expected.

show.title: What happens when the likes go away?

segments.say: Several small experiments have tried hiding the numbers, and the general picture has been consistent. People report a little less pressure about how a post will be received, and somewhat less comparison, but their overall mood and wellbeing don't change in a big way. They still look at the photos, still compare themselves, and still care how others respond. Exact results differ between studies, so it's safest to say the effect is small.

This is a pattern that we'll see again tonight. In the debate about social media, there's often a dramatic story about one feature, and then careful experiments find that changing that one feature does something modest. That doesn't mean the feature is harmless. It means that the experience of a feed is made of many parts, and removing one rarely changes the whole.

There's something moving, if you think about it, in the idea that a tap on a screen can reach a person's reward system. It says that we are, at bottom, creatures who want to be seen. That wish is not shameful. It's part of what makes us human. The question is only whether the way we are seen online fits the way we need to be.

A paper heart, a paper thumb and a scan of a brain. The study at UCLA brought all three together, and what it showed, in the end, was an old truth: approval matters to us, and our brains notice when we get it.

Four terms from this chapter. The nucleus accumbens is a region involved in reward. Social reward is the value we find in approval and belonging. The anterior cingulate cortex responds to distress, including social distress. And social proof is our tendency to follow what others seem to approve of.

show.title: Words to keep from this chapter

segments.say: If likes tug at you, a small structure can help. Many people find it useful to check reactions once or twice a day, at a time they've chosen, instead of dipping in whenever the phone buzzes. That turns an unpredictable reward into a predictable one, and the pigeon research tells us that predictable rewards are much less sticky. It's also worth remembering what the UCLA study showed, that the number itself shapes how people judge a photo. A low count may say more about timing, the algorithm or the audience than about you or your post.

show.title: A kinder way to treat likes
items: Post for the few people you'd tell in person
Check the numbers at one set time, not all day
Notice how a low count changes your mood
Remember that the count says little about the post

segments.say: If likes tug at you, you aren't being shallow. You're being a person. A useful habit is to ask who you're hoping will respond to a post, and whether their response is the one that matters. Often the answer is a handful of people, and their warmth doesn't need a number next to it.

So what did we learn? That likes activate reward circuits in teenagers, in a small but careful study. That the numbers also shape what others think. That rejection can register as distress, even from a game. And that hiding the numbers has a modest effect, because the pull comes from many parts.
In our next chapter, we'll go back to 1954, when a psychologist wrote a theory about why we look at other people to find out how we're doing, long before there was a screen to do it on.
